extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in Marc Hauser and issues of research integrity
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article summarizing the life, research, publications, and controversy (scientific misconduct investigations and findings) related to a single scientist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research misconduct: fabrication and falsification of data
rubrics_metrics.description: Found guilty of fabricating and falsifying data (Harvard internal finding; Office of Research Integrity concluded Hauser had fabricated data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page reports that fabrication and falsification are treated as research misconduct by institutions and federal agencies; such findings can lead to retraction of papers, public notices by agencies (ORI), and career consequences. Example: ORI concluded Hauser "had fabricated data, manipulated experimental results, and incorrectly described how studies were conducted."

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation/misrepresentation of experimental results and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulating experimental results and incorrectly describing how studies were conducted are cited as forms of misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ORI's findings and Harvard's inquiry treated manipulation and incorrect description of methods as serious breaches. The page cites instances where results were manipulated or study descriptions were inaccurate, prompting federal investigation and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and detail in methods/coding criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods and coding criteria must be described in sufficient detail to allow independent coding and assessment (criticized for being insufficient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics noted that "the coding criteria were described in insufficient detail to code the monkeys' behavior," which undermined the ability of others to evaluate results. Guidance implied: provide enough methodological detail for independent re-coding and verification; failure to do so is an anti-pattern that can prompt criticism and correction/retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data management and preservation (raw data/video availability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Raw data (e.g., video recordings) must be preserved and accessible; missing or stolen raw materials hinder verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes requests for remaining videotapes and the claim that other tapes had been stolen, which impeded review. Good practice: maintain and provide access to original recordings/data to support reproducibility and investigations; failure can provoke skepticism and formal inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replicability and independent replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings should be replicable; unsuccessful replication undermines original claims and can lead to retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page recounts unsuccessful replication attempts (e.g., later attempts to replicate mirror-recognition results failed) and notes a 2002 paper was later retracted. It also mentions replication/addenda published to address missing data. Guidance: robust work should survive independent replication; inability to replicate triggers further scrutiny and corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and federal investigation, transparency of findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions and federal agencies investigate alleged misconduct and may publish findings; transparency of investigations is an important expectation (and a point of criticism when lacking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harvard cooperated with ORI, NSF OIG, and the U.S. Attorney; Harvard was criticized for lack of transparency in its investigation. The page quotes that when the government concludes misconduct occurred, the federal agency makes those findings publicly available. Good practice: institutions should conduct thorough investigations and communicate outcomes appropriately; lack of transparency can erode trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions, restrictions, and required oversight after findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate sanctions may include barring from teaching, restricting types of research, requiring supervised research, and employment consequences (e.g., resignation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Hauser was barred from teaching in certain departments, resigned from his faculty position, and ORI barred him from certain types of research and required supervision for other research. These are presented as standard institutional/federal responses to confirmed misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectrum of scientific wrongdoing (degree/variety of offenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific offenses range in severity — from poor data storage to outright data fabrication — and should be considered on a spectrum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted text from The New York Times: "There is a wide spectrum of scientific sins, ranging from wrist-slap offenses like bad data storage at one end, to data fabrication at the other." This frames evaluative judgment about misconduct on a continuum, implying proportional responses depending on severity and intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of coauthors and subsequent corrective publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Coauthors can replicate work or publish addenda/replications to correct the record when problems are found with original publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes Hauser and coauthor Justin Wood replicating results and publishing them as an addendum; Proceedings of the Royal Society published a replication of missing data in an addendum. Guidance: coauthors and journals can and should facilitate corrections, replications, and addenda to address gaps or errors in the published record.
